title: Morning Edition
notes: Morning Edition for Saturday, Nov 7, 2026. It covers developments since Friday’s Morning Edition, with ongoing stories marked with their earlier dates.

The lead is Stephen Miller’s appointment as White House chief of staff, with the latest midterm count folded in. Top stories: Canada’s immigration levels plan, a construction scare at Tung Chung West station, the first foreign astronaut headed for China’s space station, the overnight strikes on Kyiv, and Paraguay’s change of president.

The U.S., Canada and World have five stories each; Hong Kong and China have four. Culture appears in the U.S. (Broadway) and Hong Kong (Shek O festival, Kusama sculpture); sports in Canada (CFL division finals, scheduled) and World (Paris Masters). China has no culture story this morning.
Two scheduled sports events (CFL division finals, Alcaraz–Ruud semifinal) are described as planned; results were not available when this edition was compiled.
provenance: Stories are compiled from the linked sources; labels describe the type of claim each story rests on.
Source pages were opened during this morning’s research; the logged check time (6:25 AM ET) was recorded at the end of that research batch rather than per page.
Xinhua and CCTV items are labelled State media. SCMP pages were partly paywalled; only their opening text was read. An AP page timed out and was not relied on.
Hong Kong’s rebuttal describes the ten-country statement in its own words; the joint statement itself was not opened here. Midterm seat totals are CBS News estimates; Donna Daily does not call races.

stories.headline: Trump names Stephen Miller White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles
stories.deck: President Trump said Friday that deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller will become chief of staff on Monday, Nov. 9, with Susie Wiles moving to his political operation — the biggest shake-up since Republicans’ midterm losses.
stories.summary: President Trump said Friday that deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller will become chief of staff on Monday, Nov. 9, with Susie Wiles moving to his political operation — the biggest shake-up since Republicans’ midterm losses. In a Truth Social post quoted by CBS News, Trump called Miller “one of my most trusted advisors” and said Wiles had done “an outstanding job.” Miller said in a statement that the mission was to “fight with all of our soul to support our President.” Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee and its likely next chair, said Miller “should lawyer up” and promised investigations. The count is still moving: CBS News estimates Democrats will hold at least 54 Senate seats and around 256 House seats in January, with more than two dozen House races and the Alaska and Mississippi Senate contests unresolved; in Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom led Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by about 1,800 votes as ballots were still being counted.
stories.why: Miller, the architect of the administration’s immigration crackdown, moves to the centre of the White House just as Democrats prepare to take both chambers and launch oversight — a sign Trump is doubling down rather than changing course.
stories.label: Official statement + reported
stories.note: Update to Thursday’s midterm-count story (Nov 6 edition). Seat totals are CBS News estimates and projections; Donna Daily does not call races. PBS also reported two more senior Justice Department resignations on Friday (National Security Division head John Eisenberg and South Florida U.S. attorney Jason Reding Quiñones).

stories.headline: U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October, far above forecasts
stories.summary: Nonfarm payrolls rose by 165,000 in October and the unemployment rate was little changed at 4.1 percent, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday. Professional and business services (+70,000), health care (+42,000) and transportation and warehousing (+25,000) led the gains, and August and September were revised up by a combined 84,000. Average hourly earnings rose 0.4 percent on the month and 3.1 percent over the year. CNBC said economists had expected about 59,000 jobs, and noted that long-term unemployment and the number of people working part time for economic reasons both rose.
stories.why: A stronger-than-expected labour market lands days after an election fought on affordability, and it raises the odds the Federal Reserve keeps pushing rates higher in December, which matters for anyone with a loan or a job hunt.
stories.label: Official figures + reported
stories.note: The BLS link is the current Employment Situation release page; BLS replaces its content with each monthly release (next: Dec 4, 2026). The forecast figure and Fed-odds context are CNBC’s.

stories.headline: Newsom moves to commute all 548 California death sentences to life without parole
stories.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced Thursday that he will commute the sentences of all 548 people on the state’s death row to life without the possibility of parole, KQED reported. More than half of the cases — those involving people with more than one felony conviction — need review by the California Supreme Court under the state constitution. The Death Penalty Information Center called it the largest act of mass clemency in U.S. history, according to KQED. In an open letter, Newsom said “we cannot execute people in our imperfect legal system and remain true to our core values.” The Criminal Justice Legal Foundation, which supports crime victims, said it is weighing a legal challenge.
stories.why: California holds the country’s largest death row, so the move — made weeks before Newsom leaves office and ahead of a widely expected presidential run — reshapes the national death-penalty debate, though the state Supreme Court still has a say in many cases.
stories.label: Official statement + reported
stories.note: Not in Friday’s edition. The commutations requiring court review are not final until the California Supreme Court acts.

stories.headline: Volunteers dig out Copperhill and McCaysville after record flooding on the Georgia–Tennessee line
stories.summary: Cleanup is under way in Copperhill, Tennessee, and McCaysville, Georgia, after 8 to 10 inches of rain pushed the Ocoee River to a record 18 feet on Thursday morning, WSMV reported. Tennessee Emergency Management said 68 people were rescued in Polk County and no deaths had been reported. Copperhill Mayor Greg Barker called it a “huge loss to our entire downtown,” with water three to five feet deep inside businesses. In McCaysville, city officials said the remaining water supply had been depleted, Atlanta News First reported late Friday; Publix and the Red Cross were handing out water and cleanup kits, and the Salvation Army planned free meals on Saturday.
stories.why: Both small towns had only just recovered from an August flood, and many owners told reporters they lack flood insurance — a reminder of how repeated extreme rain is hitting places with thin financial cushions.
stories.label: Reported + official statement
stories.note: The river is called the Toccoa in Georgia and the Ocoee in Tennessee. Rescue figures are from Tennessee officials as reported by WSMV; other outlets reported different totals for both states.

stories.headline: Buena Vista Social Club will close on Broadway Jan. 17, with a West End run planned for 2027
stories.summary: The Tony-winning musical Buena Vista Social Club will play its final Broadway performance at the Gerald Schoenfeld Theatre on Jan. 17, 2027, after 767 performances, its producers announced Friday. Playbill and Deadline reported that a West End production is planned for 2027, alongside a North American tour and engagements in Puerto Rico and Mexico City. Deadline said the show has not yet recouped its reported $17 million capitalization but producers say it is “on schedule” to do so; it grossed about $679,000 in the week ending Nov. 1. The show, with the first Broadway score performed entirely in Spanish, won five Tonys, including a special award for its onstage band, and a Grammy for its cast album. Original cast members Natalie Venetia Belcon and Ashley De La Rosa are set to return in November.
stories.why: New Yorkers have about ten weeks left to catch one of the most celebrated recent musicals, and its producers’ shift to tours and a London run shows how hit shows now earn back their money beyond Broadway.
stories.label: Reported + company figures

stories.headline: Budget immigration plan would grant permanent residency to about 657,000 people in 2027
stories.summary: Canada’s new immigration levels plan, laid out in Budget 2026, sets 380,000 new permanent residents a year for three years — but one-time measures would push the 2027 total to 657,250, CBC News reported Friday. The extra intake includes 200,000 temporary residents already living in Canada; officials said about half would come through economic streams and half on humanitarian and family grounds, including almost 32,000 people from Hong Kong and about 19,000 from Ukraine. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said Canada cannot absorb those numbers. Prime Minister Mark Carney said the plan is “in line with sustainable immigration,” citing budget figures showing international students down 71 per cent, temporary foreign workers down 57 per cent and asylum seekers down 68 per cent since 2024.
stories.why: Most of the extra permanent residents are already in Canada, so the plan changes people’s status more than population — but it puts immigration back at the centre of the budget fight and gives thousands of Hongkongers a path to stay.
stories.label: Official statement + reported
stories.note: Follows the Nov 6 edition’s Budget 2026 lead. Percent declines are the government’s figures as cited by Carney; Poilievre’s and Carney’s remarks are their positions.

stories.headline: Canada’s jobless rate rises to 6.7% as youth unemployment climbs to 13.7%
stories.summary: Employment was little changed in October (−4,700) while the unemployment rate rose 0.2 percentage points to 6.7 per cent, Statistics Canada said Friday. Youth unemployment rose 0.7 points to 13.7 per cent. Wholesale and retail trade shed 29,000 jobs, while construction and educational services added jobs. Alberta lost 24,000 jobs and its rate jumped to 7.3 per cent; Ontario’s rate also rose to 7.3 per cent. The agency also found 29.7 per cent of Canadians lived in households that had difficulty meeting their financial needs — the first year-over-year increase since 2022.
stories.why: The numbers arrive the day after a budget pitched on jobs and affordability, and the jump in young people looking for work without finding it is the part that most directly affects students and new grads.

stories.headline: Quebec pans the federal budget as Ontario and big-city mayors welcome parts of it
stories.summary: Quebec Finance Minister Nicolas Marceau said Budget 2026 “does not meet expectations” and criticized the productivity “megadeduction” for the revenue Quebec would lose if it harmonizes, CBC News reported; Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet said slower growth in health transfers would cost Quebec about $3 billion a year and that his party will vote against the budget. Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada welcomed an $11.2-billion, four-year homelessness package. In Ontario, Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy said the province supports the budget’s investment push, while Canadian Federation of Independent Business president Dan Kelly called it “mega disappointing” for small firms.
stories.why: Provincial pushback over health money and small-business complaints will shape the budget debate in Parliament — and the homelessness money is the piece most likely to be felt on city streets.
stories.label: Reported + official statement
stories.note: Ongoing: Budget 2026 was tabled Nov 5 (Nov 6 edition lead). The $3-billion figure is Blanchet’s estimate.

stories.headline: Landslide and flooding force evacuations in Zeballos on Vancouver Island
stories.summary: The village of Zeballos, home to about 125 people on Vancouver Island’s northwest coast, declared a state of local emergency on Friday after a landslide and flooding, CBC News reported. An evacuation order covers 22 properties, and the Strathcona Regional District said debris from a landslide had affected the area and it was unclear whether more slides were possible until a geotechnical assessment is complete. Ehattesaht First Nation Chief Simon John said a neighbour woke him around 3 a.m. as water poured into their yards, and linked the slide risk to a 2018 wildfire that damaged the slope above the village. Environment Canada warned this was the first of several wet and windy systems hitting the B.C. coast into next week.
stories.why: It is an early example of the fire-then-flood pattern that makes burned hillsides dangerous for years, and more storms are forecast for the B.C. coast.
stories.label: Reported + official statement

stories.headline: CFL division finals set for Saturday, with a Grey Cup spot in Calgary at stake
stories.summary: The CFL’s division finals are scheduled for Saturday, Nov. 7, Sportsnet reported. In the East final (3 p.m. ET, Percival Molson Memorial Stadium), the Montreal Alouettes (14-4), led by newly named Most Outstanding Player Davis Alexander, host the Winnipeg Blue Bombers, who are trying to become the first crossover team in league history to reach the Grey Cup; Winnipeg quarterback Zach Collaros was listed as questionable with a rib injury. In the West final (6:30 p.m. ET, Commonwealth Stadium), the Edmonton Elks (13-5), seeking their first home playoff win since 2015, host Nathan Rourke’s B.C. Lions. The winners meet in the 113th Grey Cup on Nov. 15 at McMahon Stadium in Calgary.
stories.why: Either a historic crossover run or two long droughts could end on Saturday, and the results set up Canada’s biggest single sporting event of the fall.
stories.label: Reported

stories.headline: Hong Kong government rebuts ten-country statement on Joshua Wong’s sentence
stories.summary: The Hong Kong government issued a statement on Saturday expressing “strong dissatisfaction” with a joint statement by ten countries — the United States, United Kingdom, France, Germany, Japan, Italy, Australia, Canada, the Netherlands and New Zealand — about the sentencing of activist Joshua Wong (Wong Chi-fung) in a national security case. A government spokesperson said the statement “deliberately distorted facts,” noted that Wong pleaded guilty to conspiracy to collude with foreign forces, said the court acted independently, and urged the countries to stop interfering in what it called China’s internal affairs. The Legislative Council issued a separate statement condemning what it called external smears.
stories.why: The widening diplomatic row — now including Canada and Japan — keeps Hong Kong’s national security cases at the centre of its relations with Western governments.
stories.label: Official statement
stories.note: Ongoing: Wong’s 10-year sentence and the first Western reactions were in the Nov 6 edition. The ten-country statement itself was not opened in this run; its content is described here only as characterized by the Hong Kong government.

stories.headline: MTR halts unauthorised pillar repairs at the unfinished Tung Chung West station
stories.summary: The MTR Corporation ordered a contractor to stop work after finding that the tops of some platform-level columns at the under-construction Tung Chung West station had been filled in without approval, TVB News and Dimsum Daily reported on Saturday. The reports followed an HK01 investigation saying about half of roughly 60 concourse-level pillars appear to stop 20 to 30 centimetres short of the ceiling. The MTR did not directly address that claim, but said the issue does not affect structural safety, that the Bouygues–Dragages joint venture must submit a full report and an approved fix before resuming, and that remedial costs fall on the contractor. Engineers quoted by TVB disagreed on whether gaps are a normal construction stage or a procedural error.
stories.why: The station is part of a roughly HK$19.5-billion line extension due to open in 2029, and it follows an earlier counterfeit-tile report at Tung Chung East on the same project — so residents will want clear answers on quality control.
stories.label: Reported + official statement
stories.note: The “half the pillars” figure comes from HK01’s report and sources, as relayed by Dimsum Daily; the MTR has not confirmed it. HK01’s original article was not opened in this run.

stories.headline: Shek O villages stage their once-a-decade Tai Ping Ching Chiu parade
stories.summary: Three villages around Shek O — Shek O Village, Big Wave Bay Village and Hok Tsui Tsuen — held their decennial Tai Ping Ching Chiu parade on Saturday, TVB News reported. The procession set off at 10:30 a.m. from a bamboo theatre near Shek O Beach, with children dressed as figures such as the warrior Mu Guiying, the folk deity Nezha and the Tang consort Lady Yang. Cantonese opera and rituals meant to ward off plague followed in the afternoon. Police closed parts of Shek O Road and Big Wave Bay Road from 6 a.m. to 11 p.m., and Citybus ran special X9 services from Central, The Standard reported.
stories.why: Festivals held only once every ten years are some of the city’s rarest living traditions; this one won’t come round again for another decade.
stories.label: Reported

stories.headline: A Pakistani astronaut will be the first foreigner to visit China’s space station
stories.summary: A Pakistani astronaut will fly on China’s Shenzhou-24 crewed mission as a payload specialist, the China Manned Space Agency said on Saturday, according to state news agency Xinhua. The astronaut is to make a short stay in orbit and return to Earth aboard Shenzhou-23, making the mission the first joint flight of Chinese and foreign astronauts in China’s human spaceflight programme. China and Pakistan signed an astronaut-selection agreement in February 2025; Xinhua said two Pakistani reserve astronauts were chosen, one to fly and one as backup. No launch date was given in the report.
stories.why: Opening Tiangong to a partner country’s astronaut is a soft-power milestone for Beijing, which is building its own orbital partnerships as the International Space Station nears retirement.
stories.label: State media + official statement
stories.note: Sourced to Xinhua (state media) relaying the China Manned Space Agency. The astronaut was not named in the report.

stories.headline: Beijing voices “serious concern” over U.S. sanctions in call with Bessent and Greer before APEC
stories.summary: Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng raised “serious concern” about recent U.S. restrictions on China in a video call on Friday with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, the South China Morning Post reported, citing Xinhua. China’s Commerce Ministry said it “firmly opposes” new U.S. sanctions on two Chinese companies. Both sides described the talks as “frank, in-depth and constructive” and agreed to manage differences, according to Xinhua. A new round of trade talks is expected in Shenzhen later this month, before Xi Jinping and Donald Trump meet on the sidelines of the APEC summit there. Separately, the Guardian reported that a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said Beijing is “in communication with relevant parties” about a possible Xi–Trump–Putin meeting.
stories.why: The Shenzhen APEC summit is shaping up as the biggest test of U.S.–China relations this year, and a three-way meeting with Putin — if it happens — would also put Ukraine on the table.

stories.headline: China passes a cross-border corruption law as lawmakers weigh limits on a secretive detention measure
stories.summary: China’s top legislature, the National People’s Congress Standing Committee, adopted a 47-article law against cross-border corruption on Friday, state news agency Xinhua reported, covering case handling, international cooperation and corporate compliance. At the same session lawmakers ratified an agreement establishing a World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization and removed Li Lecheng as minister of industry and information technology. Separately, the South China Morning Post reported that a draft amendment to the Criminal Procedure Law sent to the legislature for initial review would narrow “residential surveillance at a designated location,” a form of detention that critics say has become the harshest tool in state-security cases.
stories.why: The corruption law gives Beijing a legal basis to pursue fugitives and assets abroad and adds compliance duties for Chinese firms overseas, while any curbs on secret detention would be a rare move in the other direction — the details will matter.
stories.label: State media + reported
stories.note: The detention change is a draft at first review, not law. SCMP is partly paywalled; only its summary was read.

stories.headline: Giant pandas from China make their public debut at Zoo Atlanta
stories.summary: Six-year-old giant pandas Ping Ping and Fu Shuang went on public view at Zoo Atlanta on Friday, CBS Atlanta reported, nearly two years after the zoo’s previous pandas returned to China. The pair arrived in late September and spent time in quarantine before the debut, which drew crowds to an upgraded habitat with larger indoor areas, pools and climbing structures. Under an agreement with the China Wildlife Conservation Association, they are expected to stay for 10 years. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said the partnership would strengthen ties between the Chinese and American people. Zoo Atlanta joins the National Zoo and San Diego Zoo as the three U.S. zoos with giant pandas.
stories.why: Panda loans are one of Beijing’s oldest diplomatic tools, and their return to a third U.S. zoo is a small but visible sign of warmer people-to-people ties ahead of the Xi–Trump meeting.
stories.label: Reported + official statement

stories.headline: Russian missiles hit Kyiv’s power grid and a Dnipro bridge days before Abu Dhabi talks
stories.summary: Russia launched 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and other regions overnight into Saturday, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, damaging energy facilities, homes, a kindergarten building and the Northern (Pivnichnyi) Bridge over the Dnipro, which was temporarily closed, RFE/RL reported. Five people were injured in Kyiv, including a 14-year-old, and Mayor Vitali Klitschko called the capital’s energy supply “extremely difficult,” with parts of the city losing power, heat and water. Russia’s Defence Ministry confirmed the bridge strike, claiming it was used to move weapons. The attack comes before planned U.S.–Ukraine–Russia talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10–11.
stories.why: Strikes on bridges and power just before winter and before the first three-way peace talks since February show how both sides are trying to shape the negotiations on the battlefield.
stories.label: Reported + official statement + claim
stories.note: Ongoing: the Nov 6 edition reported Zelenskyy’s warning about attacks on power plants. Drone and missile totals are Ukrainian figures; Russia’s justification for the bridge strike is its claim.

stories.headline: Paraguay’s Senate removes President Santiago Peña over a bank collapse; Pedro Alliana sworn in
stories.summary: Paraguay’s Senate voted 44–0, with one abstention, to remove President Santiago Peña on Friday, and Vice-President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as the country’s 53rd president, Al Jazeera and the Guardian reported. Prosecutors then placed Peña under house arrest. The crisis began when the central bank seized Ueno Bank, which it said had fallen below solvency rules, freezing the accounts of about 2.9 million customers — roughly 60 per cent of adults, according to the Guardian — and setting off protests. Prosecutors are investigating Peña for suspected illicit enrichment, money laundering and influence peddling over his ties to the bank; he has said he will cooperate, and his lawyers argued he was given too little time to mount a defence.
stories.why: A banking failure that cut most of a country off from its own money brought down a sitting president within days — a stark example of how financial regulation failures become political ones.
stories.label: Reported + allegation
stories.note: The accusations against Peña are under investigation and unproven. Outlets give slightly different customer totals (about 2.9 million vs roughly three million).

stories.headline: Hoax bomb threats disrupt at least 18 more flights across Europe
stories.summary: A fresh wave of bomb threats on Friday affected at least 18 flights to or from Bulgaria, Cyprus, Czechia, France, Hungary, Italy, Portugal, Romania and the U.K., the Guardian reported; all landed safely and no explosives were found. Earlier threats on Tuesday and Thursday had forced at least 35 flights to divert or be searched, and Hungary scrambled fighter jets to escort civilian planes. Media organizations in Ireland, including RTÉ, also received threats that disrupted broadcasts. Investigators said there was no evidence so far that a terror group or state was behind the hoaxes; Spain’s foreign minister called it a likely “attempt at hybrid aggression.” The BBC counted 32 threats affecting a dozen airlines in four days.
stories.why: Even hoaxes can ground planes, scramble jets and empty newsrooms, and European officials are treating the pattern as possible hybrid warfare — a growing risk for anyone flying in Europe this season.
stories.label: Reported + official statement
stories.note: Counts differ between outlets (Guardian: at least 18 on Friday and 35 earlier; BBC: 32 threats over four days). Who is responsible is unknown.

stories.headline: Pope Leo begins a 12-day Latin America tour in Uruguay, weeks after surgery
stories.summary: Pope Leo XIV landed in Montevideo on Friday to begin a 12-day trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, Vatican News reported, his sixth international journey. The programme includes stops in Buenos Aires, Córdoba and Luján before Lima, Chiclayo, Cusco and Pucallpa in Peru, about a dozen flights and nearly 40 addresses in Spanish, running through Nov. 17. PBS NewsHour noted that the trip comes three weeks after the 71-year-old pope had lung cancer surgery, and that Peru is a homecoming: he served there for more than two decades and became a naturalized citizen.
stories.why: The pope’s return to the region where he spent much of his career is a test of his health after surgery and a big moment for Latin America’s Catholics.
stories.label: Reported + official statement

stories.headline: Alcaraz saves two match points to beat Fritz and reach the Paris Masters semifinals
stories.summary: Carlos Alcaraz came back to beat Taylor Fritz 6-7(10), 7-5, 6-3 on Friday night at the Rolex Paris Masters, saving two match points in the second set to reach the tournament’s semifinals for the first time, the ATP Tour reported. The result ended Fritz’s hopes of qualifying for the ATP Finals and secured the eighth and final place in Turin for Spain’s Rafael Jodar. Alcaraz is scheduled to face Casper Ruud, who beat Nuno Borges 7-6(5), 6-4, in Saturday’s semifinal.
stories.why: It was one of the comebacks of the season and it settled the field for the ATP Finals in Turin on Nov. 15–22.
stories.label: Reported
stories.note: The Alcaraz–Ruud semifinal had not been played when this edition was compiled.
